summary: 94/18 provides the first quoted example in the existing empty Infectum box: plural stonecutters act on stones, resumed by -nne. Preserve nḥt 2, distinct from descending nḥt 1.
naḥote occurs as recipient, agent and possessor of tools. These are professional nouns naming stonecutters; no verbal Part act. paradigm can be established from their syntax or qattāl-like shape.
11/16 d naḥit modifies stones and denotes dressed stone, but may be a borrowed technical adjective or nominal expression. It does not securely establish a Turoyo Part. Pass. box.
No new sense is needed: the finite konəḥtənne directly confirms inherited to hew (stones). The edition’s German is retained even though the existing entry gloss is English.
The Jan stoneworking set has both t and d spellings: nḥite versus nḥide, and finite nəḥdiwo/nəḥadwo. Preserve all source tokens; do not infer a dialect law from this small set.

Plural nḥite/nḥide with kefe supplies agreement missing from the ambiguous round 1 d naḥit. This supports a Detransitive Part. Pass. proposal while leaving native-versus-borrowed morphology open. No finite Detransitive box is asserted.
naḥode is an occupational noun in lists with qaṭoʕe d kefe and maʕmərone. Its coordination and profession context support the round 1 exclusion of naḥote from Part act.
Is d naḥit at 11/16 a borrowed Arabic adjective, a stoneworking noun phrase or a verbal Part. Pass.? Explain its apparent absence of plural agreement before adding a form box.
Is naḥote a lexical profession noun or a productive verb-derived nominal form? Supply finite or predicative evidence before classifying it as Part act.
Are nḥite/nḥide native result forms, borrowed technical adjectives, or both? Is their plural agreement productive?
Confirm t/d in nəḥdiwo/nəḥadwo and nḥide; do these reflect pronunciation, transcription or lexical variants?
Jan finite nəḥdiwo/nəḥadwo confirms round 1 hewing for construction. The newly proposed result forms are related to this same lexical operation, distinct from nḥt 1 descent.
